summary: Gives an overview of Source-Specific Multicast and issues around deploying it. It covers how this service model eases the challenges of inter-domain multicast, what changes routing protocols and applications need, and interoperability issues. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of listening to everyone sending to a group, you pick one sender to follow. This memo explains how that simpler idea helps broadcast-style delivery work across the internet.

subtitle: Multicast where a receiver names the one sender it wants, which sidesteps address allocation and shared trees.

tldr.problem: Any-Source Multicast makes inter-domain deployment hard: group addresses collide, any host can send to a group, and shared trees need extra machinery.
tldr.mechanism: Source-Specific Multicast defines a channel as a source S plus a group address G. Receivers subscribe to (S,G) using IGMPv3 or MLDv2, and PIM-SM builds source-rooted trees only.
tldr.outcome: SSM removes the need for global group address allocation, rendezvous points and MSDP, and makes spamming a channel harder. This overview is not a standard.

facts.label: Channel
facts.value: Source S plus SSM address G

today: RFC 3569 is an Informational overview from July 2003. The metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC, and the document itself says it is not a standard for SSM.

sections.title: What SSM Is
sections.content:
Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) offers a network-layer service called a channel. A channel is identified by a source IP address S and an SSM destination address G. The source sends datagrams to G, and a receiver subscribes to the channel (S,G). IPv4 has an address range reserved by IANA for SSM, and IPv6 already has one.

Subscriptions use IGMP version 3 for IPv4 and MLD version 2 for IPv6. The tree for forwarding is rooted at the source S and built with PIM Sparse Mode. The RFC says it is not a standard. It is an introduction to SSM and its benefits for anyone planning to deploy it, with pointers to more detailed documents.
sections.plainLanguage: A channel is like a TV station: one sender, many viewers. You tell the network which sender you want.

sections.title: Service Models and Today's ASM Setup
sections.content:
In Any-Source Multicast (ASM), from RFC 1112, a datagram goes to a host group identified by one destination address (224.0.0.0 through 239.255.255.255 for IPv4). Hosts may join and leave at any time, and any host may send to the group, even if it is not a member. Source-Filtered Multicast (SFM) keeps the same address range but lets a receiver ask for data from only certain sources, or from all but certain sources, using IGMPv3 or MLDv2.

The common ASM suite is IGMPv2, PIM-SM, MSDP and MBGP. PIM-SM builds a shared tree rooted at a rendezvous point (RP) within a domain. Between domains, RPs use MSDP to announce sources, and MBGP carries multicast routing information. The RFC notes that hosts with SFM support were not widely available at the time of writing.
sections.plainLanguage: In the old way, a room full of people can all shout into one microphone. The new way gives each speaker their own microphone, and you choose whom to hear.

sections.title: Problems SSM Solves
sections.content:
The RFC lists three deployment problems with ASM, each of which SSM addresses.

  • Address allocation. ASM has no deployable way to stop different applications from picking the same group address. In SSM the channel (S1,G) differs from (S2,G), so each source is responsible for avoiding collisions among its own channels.
  • Access control. In ASM a receiver cannot choose its sources, and a source cannot stop others from using its group address. In SSM a receiver gets data only from S, and a sender on (S,G) is automatically the only one on that channel, barring address spoofing. That makes spamming a channel much harder.
  • Well-known sources. When the source is known in advance, shared trees are unnecessary. SSM needs only source-based trees, so neither the RP-based shared tree of PIM-SM nor MSDP is required. Use of MBGP is the same for ASM and SSM.
sections.plainLanguage: With SSM, every sender has their own mailbox name, so nobody mixes up addresses, and strangers cannot drop junk into your channel.

sections.title: The SSM Framework
sections.content:
The RFC breaks the end-to-end design into elements. Address allocation: IANA assigned 232/8 for IPv4 and FF3x::/96 is used for IPv6. IGMPv3 and MLDv2 do not limit (S,G) joins to that range, but SSM service is defined only there for IPv4.

Channel discovery: a receiver application must know both S and G before subscribing. Finding them is the application's job, for example through web pages or session announcements, and the mechanism is outside the scope of the RFC. SSM-aware applications must be able to give both addresses to the host's network layer.

Host reporting: IGMP version 2 and MLD version 1 let a host name only a group. IGMPv3 and MLDv2 add source filtering, and IGMPv3 provides a superset of what SSM needs.
sections.plainLanguage: To watch a channel you need two things: who is sending and the channel name. Another tool, like a web page, tells you those.

sections.title: PIM-SSM Routing Rules
sections.content:
Router requirements for the SSM address range are mainly about preventing ASM-style behavior there. Only a small subset of PIM-SM is needed for SSM. The most important changes are:

  • When a designated router (DR) gets an (S,G) join with G in the SSM range, it MUST start an (S,G) join and never a (*,G) join.
  • Backbone routers MUST NOT propagate (*,G) joins for SSM-range groups.
  • Rendezvous Points MUST NOT accept PIM Register messages or (*,G) Join messages in the SSM range.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules tell routers to build a path straight back to the one chosen sender, and never to use the old shared meeting point.

sections.title: Living Alongside ASM
sections.content:
SSM is the only service model for the SSM address range, while ASM continues for the rest. A receiver can send an (S,G) join outside the SSM range, but then it is not guaranteed SSM service. MSDP is not needed for SSM but is needed for ASM, so RPs must not accept, originate or forward MSDP SA messages for the SSM range.

On security, the RFC says SSM adds no new security considerations for IP multicast. It can help prevent denial-of-service from unwanted sources sending to a channel, though no guarantee is given.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ways work side by side: one set of channel numbers is for pick-your-sender, and the rest stay as they were.
